scenes.heading: Physiology and homeostasis
scenes.sub: Keeping the inside steady when the outside changes
scenes.say: Your cells only work within a narrow range of temperature, pH and water balance, yet the world outside keeps changing. How do a frog, a fish, a kangaroo and an insect all solve this problem?

scenes.heading: Some Sensible Cats Eat Rice
steps: Control centre: compares to set point
scenes.say: Every feedback loop runs: stimulus, sensor, control centre, effector, response. Some sensible cats eat rice. Negative feedback is a thermostat: it reverses the change. Positive feedback is a snowball: it amplifies the change until the event is finished, as in childbirth.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A house with the heater on all winter: steady, but a huge power bill
scenes.science: Endotherms make their own heat, at a high energy cost
scenes.breaks: Ectotherms aren't always cold: a basking lizard can be warmer than a mammal, and endotherms use behaviour too.
scenes.say: An endotherm is like a house with the heater on all winter: a steady temperature, but a huge power bill. An ectotherm is like you warming up on the beach after a cold swim. The heat is free, but you depend on the sun, so a lizard basks in the morning and shelters at midday.

scenes.heading: Mouse vs lizard
scenes.question: As air cools from 30 °C to 10 °C, the mouse stays at 37 °C. Its O₂ use rises from 2.0 to 5.0 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹. Why?
lines: Lizard body temp tracks the air
scenes.say: In a cold chamber, the lizard's body temperature tracks the air. The mouse holds thirty-seven degrees. As the air cools, the mouse loses heat faster, so its oxygen use climbs from two to five millilitres per gram per hour: a two and a half fold rise.
scenes.caption: In a cold chamber, the lizard's body temperature tracks the air. The mouse holds 37 °C. As the air cools, the mouse loses heat faster, so its O₂ use climbs from 2.0 to 5.0 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹: a 2.5-fold rise.

scenes.heading: Fish and salt
scenes.say: Salty sea, sip and save. Fresh water, flush away. Marine fish lose water, so they drink seawater, pump salt out at the gills and make little urine. Freshwater fish gain water, so they drink little and make lots of dilute urine.

scenes.heading: Nitrogen waste
points: Ammonia: most toxic, needs lots of water
Urea: less toxic, can be concentrated
Uric acid: a paste, very little water
scenes.say: Nitrogen waste goes from wettest to driest. Ammonia is very toxic, so aquatic animals flush it away with lots of water. Mammals make urea, which is less toxic. Birds, many reptiles and insects make uric acid, a paste that needs very little water.

scenes.heading: Hearts count up 2, 3, 3, 4
scenes.say: Vertebrate hearts count up two, three, three, four. Fish have two chambers and a single circuit. Amphibians and most reptiles have three. Birds and mammals have four, with fully separated double circulation that keeps pressure high for their busy metabolism.

points: Sea: sip and save; fresh: flush away
scenes.say: Quick recap. Feedback loops run from stimulus to response, and most homeostasis uses negative feedback. Endotherms pay for steady heat. Marine fish sip and save, freshwater fish flush. Nitrogen waste goes ammonia, urea, uric acid. Now try the practice questions!
